profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between the backend platform team and developer-experience tooling team at a mid-sized software company that is modernizing an internal legacy workflow: they are wiring CVS commit events into an Elvin-based notification bus and a desktop tickertape/chat client so developers can see commit activity and talk inline about code changes. The immediate context is a pilot rollout for two product teams that still rely on CVS mirrors for part of their release process. The agenda is to align on the event interface, what metadata gets forwarded from CVS into notifications, who handles message formatting and retention, and what each side needs to deliver before a Thursday pilot check-in. The expected outcome is a shared plan for the integration handoff: what the platform team will emit, what the tooling team will render/store, and what counts as the integration being 'ready' for the pilot.

members.name: Nina Patel
members.expertise: Source control integrations, event pipelines, internal developer infrastructure
members.background: Nina has spent six years maintaining the company's repository adapters and build-event services; she recently added the CVS hook that publishes commit data into the internal Elvin notification cluster.
members.private_state: She wants to keep the integration thin so her team does not inherit long-term ownership of chat semantics or client-side formatting, and she is worried about reopening the CVS hook code right before the pilot.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the commit 'message' should appear in tickertape, the payload can remain the raw CVS log text plus filenames, because presentation concerns belong to the client.
The 'staging bus' for this pilot means the shared internal Elvin cluster already used by other low-risk dev tools, not a separate isolated channel per pilot team.

If the integration is called 'ready', that means commit events arrive end-to-end in the client for normal commits; edge cases like amend-like bursts, reconnect behavior, or chat threading can be cleaned up after the pilot.
The tooling team will own any deduplication or grouping of rapid CVS file-level events into a single human-readable item, since the backend emits repository facts, not conversation objects.

members.name: Leo Martinez
members.expertise: Developer tools UX, team chat workflows, desktop clients and notification design
members.background: Leo joined from a collaboration-tools startup and now leads the internal tickertape client refresh, including chat affordances layered onto system notifications for engineering teams.
members.private_state: He wants the pilot to look polished enough to win approval for a wider rollout, and he is concerned that noisy or cryptic commit traffic will make the chat client seem low-quality.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the commit 'message' in tickertape, they mean a concise, already-normalized line suitable for humans, with noisy file-level fragments collapsed before it reaches the client.
The 'staging bus' for the pilot means a dedicated Elvin topic space for the two pilot teams so they can test without unrelated commit traffic or accidental subscriber overlap.

If the integration is 'ready', that means the pilot users can rely on it as a communication surface: grouped commit posts are readable, reconnects do not replay confusing duplicates, and basic availability/chat context works.

Because the platform team owns the CVS hook and Elvin publisher, it will also stamp stable event IDs and grouping keys that the client can use, rather than forcing the client to infer structure from raw payloads.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the commit message
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the tickertape should show the CVS commit message.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the raw CVS log entry emitted from the hook, potentially accompanied by per-file records and unchanged original text.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a single normalized, human-readable summary line for one logical commit, already cleaned up for display.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In source-control integration work, 'commit message' sounds like a settled, obvious term; both expect the other to share the standard meaning from their own layer, so neither sees a reason to unpack whether it is raw archival text or presentation-ready text.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to wire the pilot to staging first.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the existing shared Elvin staging cluster used across internal dev infrastructure.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the dedicated pilot-only Elvin namespace his team set up for the new tickertape client.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both teams already have something informally called 'staging' in daily use; because each option is plausible and both are non-production, the phrase feels specific enough and does not trigger clarification.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree on getting the integration ready for Thursday's pilot check-in.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes 'ready' means successful transport of representative CVS events into the client during normal operation, with rough edges acceptable for pilot feedback.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes 'ready' means the experience is stable and legible enough that pilot users can treat it as a usable coordination tool, including sane grouping and duplicate handling.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Coordination meetings often use milestone language like 'ready' or 'good for pilot' as shorthand; both are cooperative and optimistic, so they interpret the phrase through their own team's quality bar without realizing the mismatch.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that rapid CVS events should be grouped so the ticker is not noisy.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the backend will continue to emit file-level events and the client will group them by time window and author.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the publisher will emit stable commit/group identifiers so the client only renders already-groupable logical events.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They agree on the outcome—less noise—so the implementation boundary goes unspoken; ownership of grouping logic feels like an obvious consequence of each person's existing system architecture, making the difference easy to miss.

If events get from the hook through the bus into tickertape for ordinary commits, that's ready enough for the pilot check-in. I do not want my team reopening the hook for chat-centric semantics or polishing edge cases this late.
